title: When stopping breaks the rule
objectives: Check the conditions of optional stopping, and see why doubling up cannot beat a fair game.

screens.title: Stop when ahead
screens.prose: A fair walk from 0 stops the first time you are up £1. The fair walk always comes back to any level (The coin-flip walk), so it reaches $+1$ with chance 1. Some paths take a very long time.
screens.question: What is $E[S_T]$, your expected winnings when you stop?

hints.text: Where is every path when it stops?
Each path stops at $+1$, the first time it gets there.

feedback.correct: £1, yet $S_0 = 0$: stopping has changed the mean.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Every path stops at $+1$.

byKey.ost: You applied optional stopping without checking its conditions. Every path stops at $+1$, so the mean at the stop is 1.

explain.text: Every path stops at $+1$, so $E[S_T] = 1 \ne 0 = S_0$. A fair game has been beaten, so one of the theorem's conditions must fail. The rest of this lesson finds which one.

screens.title: Add a floor
screens.prose: Now add a floor: you also stop if you are down £$L$. Here 300 games start with the floor at $-9$. Slide the floor down and watch the average of $S_T$ and the average length.

derive.caption: {{values.hitsUp}} of {{values.paths}} reached +£1. Average of $S_T$: {{fixed(values.stopped, 2)}}. Average length: {{fixed(values.tauMean, 1)}} bets.

screens.question: With the floor at $-9$, what is the chance of reaching $+1$ first?

hints.text: Shift up by 9: you start at 9 with ends at 0 and 10.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Shift by 9 and use $\tfrac{i}{N}$.

byKey.one: Without the floor it is 1. With it, a run of nine losses stops some games first.
byKey.half: The floor is 9 away and the target 1, so the target is much likelier.
byKey.tenth: That is the chance of hitting the floor.

explain.text: The chance is $\tfrac{L}{L+1} = \tfrac{9}{10}$, so $E[S_T] = \tfrac{9}{10} \times 1 - \tfrac{1}{10} \times 9 = 0$. Here 276 of 300 games reached +£1 and $S_T$ averaged 0.20. The rare loss of £9 exactly cancels the frequent gains of £1.

screens.title: The price of the floor
screens.prose: The floor keeps the game fair, but at a cost in time. Slide the floor and read the average length.

derive.caption: {{values.hitsUp}} of {{values.paths}} reached +£1. Average of $S_T$: {{fixed(values.stopped, 2)}}. Average length: {{fixed(values.tauMean, 1)}} bets.

screens.question: With the floor at $-L$, how many bets does a game last on average? Give your answer for $L = 9$.

feedback.correct: $E[T] = L$: 9 bets here, 99 with the floor at $-99$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Shift by $L$ and use $i(N - i)$.

byKey.ten: $N = L + 1 = 10$ is the width. The formula is $i(N - i) = 9 \times 1$.
byKey.sq: $81 = L^2$ would hold from the middle. You start next to the target.
byKey.one: 1 bet is the shortest game, not the average.

explain.text: $E[T] = L$: 9 bets at $L = 9$ (this batch averaged 8.7), and 99 at $L = 99$. At $L = 99$ the batch shows only about 40, because the mean comes from rare games lasting thousands of bets. As the floor drops the mean of $S_T$ stays 0, while the expected time grows without bound.

screens.title: What broke
screens.prose: With no floor, $E[T] = \lim L = \infty$, and the walk may fall any distance before it reaches $+1$. Recall the three conditions: $T$ bounded; $E[T]$ finite with bounded steps; the stopped walk bounded with $T$ finite.
screens.question: Without a floor, which conditions of optional stopping fail? Select all that apply.

options.text: $T$ is not bounded
$E[T]$ is infinite
The stopped walk is not bounded below
The walk is not a martingale
options.why: Each bet is still fair. The walk is a martingale; the stopping rule is the problem.

hints.text: No cap on time, $E[T] = \infty$, and no floor.
All three conditions fail, and the walk is still a martingale.

feedback.correct: All three fail, so the theorem says nothing, and indeed $E[S_T] = 1$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each condition fails here; the walk itself is fine.

byKey.mart: The walk is fair. Only the stopping time breaks the rule.

explain.text: $T$ can be any length, its mean is $\lim L = \infty$, and the walk can sink without limit first. With every condition gone, the theorem gives no promise. The gain of £1 is paid for by unbounded time and unbounded losses on the way.

screens.title: A cap on time
screens.prose: Instead of a floor, cap the time: stop when up £1 or after 100 bets. Now $T \le 100$ is bounded, so $E[S_T] = 0$. By the reflection count, the walk fails to reach $+1$ in 100 bets with chance $\binom{100}{50} / 2^{100}$.
screens.question: Fill in the chance of failing, and the average winnings when it fails.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute the chance, then use $E[S_T] = 0$.

explain.text: The cap makes $T$ bounded, so the mean at the stop is 0. You win £1 with chance 0.9204, and the other 0.0796 of games end down about £11.56. These 300 games averaged +0.07, with 20 failing.

screens.title: The doubling system
screens.prose: The casino's original martingale: bet £1, double after each loss, stop at the first win. With £1,023 you can afford ten bets, since $1 + 2 + \dots + 512 = 1023$. Any win recovers every loss plus £1. If all ten lose, you lose £1,023.

state.caption: One cycle at a fair coin: win £1 with chance 1023/1024, lose £1,023 with chance 1/1024.

screens.question: What is the expected gain of one cycle with a fair coin?

hints.text: All ten bets lose with chance $(\tfrac12)^{10} = \tfrac{1}{1024}$.

feedback.correct: £0. $T \le 10$ is bounded, so the theorem holds.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Weight the £1 win and the £1,023 loss by their chances.

byKey.win: You counted only the usual outcome. The rare loss is sized to cancel it.
byKey.most: $\tfrac{1023}{1024} \approx 0.999$ is the chance of the win, not the expected gain.
byKey.loss: That is the loss in the bad case, which has chance only 1 in 1,024.

explain.text: $1 \times \tfrac{1023}{1024} - 1023 \times \tfrac{1}{1024} = 0$. The cycle stops within 10 bets, a bounded stopping time, so it cannot beat a fair coin. A seeded run of 200,000 fair cycles averaged +£0.032, because one cycle has sd about £32.

screens.title: Doubling at a real wheel
screens.prose: At red on a European wheel each bet wins with chance $\tfrac{18}{37}$. All ten bets now lose with chance $(\tfrac{19}{37})^{10}$.

state.caption: One cycle at red: win £1 with chance 1 − (19/37)^10, lose £1,023 otherwise.

screens.question: What is the expected gain of one cycle? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use the chance $(\tfrac{19}{37})^{10}$ that all ten lose.

byKey.fair: With a fair coin it is 0. Here every bet has the casino's edge.
byKey.spin: $-\tfrac{1}{37}$ is the edge on one £1 spin. A cycle stakes up to £1,023.
byKey.loss: That is the loss in the bad case, not the average.
byKey.sign: 1 − 1024(19/37)¹⁰ is below zero, because the rare loss of £1,023 outweighs the £1 gain. A positive 0.3056 books the expected loss as a gain.

explain.text: $1 - 1024(\tfrac{19}{37})^{10} \approx -0.3056$; summing the ten winning branches and the losing one gives the same. Doubling cannot turn a supermartingale into a winner. It only moves the losses into one rare, large event.

screens.title: Unlimited money
screens.prose: Suppose you had unlimited money. The cycle ends at the first win, after $T$ bets with $E[T] = 2$. The stake on that bet is $2^{T - 1}$, with mean $\sum_k (\tfrac12)^k 2^{k - 1} = \tfrac12 + \tfrac12 + \dots$, which is infinite. The panel plays doubling from £1,023 again and again.
screens.question: With unlimited money, which condition of optional stopping fails?

options.text: The steps are not bounded: the last stake has infinite mean
$T$ is not bounded, so nothing can be said
options.why: Condition (2) allows unbounded $T$ when $E[T]$ is finite. Here $E[T] = 2$, so look at the steps.

options.text: $E[T]$ is infinite
options.why: $E[T] = 2$: the first win comes quickly. The stakes are the problem.

options.text: The bankroll is not a martingale
options.why: Every bet is fair whatever its size, so the bankroll is a martingale.

hints.text: Go through the conditions: is $T$ bounded? Is $E[T]$ finite? Are the steps bounded?
$E[T] = 2$ is finite, but a stake of $2^{T-1}$ has no bound.
Condition (2) fails on its second half: the steps are unbounded.

feedback.correct: The steps are unbounded, so a sure £1 is possible only with infinite money.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. $E[T]$ is finite; check the size of the steps.

byKey.mart: Fair bets of any size keep the bankroll fair.

explain.text: $E[T] = 2$ is finite, but the stakes have no bound, so condition (2) fails. That is how unlimited doubling wins £1 for sure. With a real bankroll the panel climbs by £1 a cycle, then a run of losses wipes it out.

screens.title: One in 1,024
screens.prose: A colleague backtests the £1,023 doubling system on a fair coin. It wins £1 in almost every cycle. She argues that ten losses in a row has chance 1 in 1,024, so the system is safe and profitable.

state.caption: Win £1 with chance 1023/1024; lose £1,023 with chance 1/1024.

screens.question: What is wrong with her argument?

options.text: Nothing: a 1-in-1,024 loss is too rare to matter
options.why: You weighed the chance but not the size. The loss is 1,023 times the gain.

options.text: The rare loss is sized to cancel the gains exactly, so the mean is 0
After many wins, a loss becomes more likely
options.why: Each cycle is independent of the last. The coin has no memory.

options.text: The system fails only because the casino may close
options.why: The loss comes from the bankroll limit, not from opening hours.

hints.text: Multiply each outcome by its chance.
They are equal, so the expected gain is exactly 0.

feedback.correct: Right: the loss is rare but exactly large enough to cancel the gains.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the chance times the size for each outcome.

byKey.safe: You compared chances only. A loss of £1,023 with chance 1 in 1,024 costs as much as the gains bring.
byKey.streak: Past wins do not change the next cycle.
byKey.time: Even with endless time, the expected gain per cycle stays 0.

explain.text: The loss has chance $\tfrac{1}{1024}$ and size £1,023, so it costs about £0.999 a cycle on average. The gains bring the same. A backtest without the loss looks profitable until the rare loss arrives.

widget.solution:
import random
from fractions import Fraction

def doubling_ev(doublings, p):
    """Exact expected gain of one doubling cycle: bet 1, 2, 4, ...
    for at most `doublings` bets, each won with chance p, with a
    bankroll of 2**doublings - 1."""
    p = Fraction(p)
    lose_all = (1 - p) ** doublings
    return (1 - lose_all) * 1 - lose_all * (2 ** doublings - 1)

def stop_when_up(max_steps, trials, seed):
    """Simulate a fair walk from 0 that stops at +1 or after
    max_steps steps. Return (share that reached +1, mean final value)."""
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    reached = 0
    total = 0
    for _ in range(trials):
        s = 0
        for _ in range(max_steps):
            s += 1 if rng.random() < 0.5 else -1
            if s == 1:
                break
        reached += s == 1
        total += s
    return reached / trials, total / trials
widget.how: Check runs 9 hidden tests. The doubling cases compare exact fractions. Three walk cases use fixed seeds, so draw one `rng.random()` per step and step up when it is below 0.5.

hints.text: The cycle loses everything only if all $d$ bets lose, with chance $(1 - p)^d$.
For the walk: loop `max_steps` times, add `+1 if rng.random() < 0.5 else -1`, and break when the walk reaches 1.

feedback.correct: All pass: the fair cycle is worth exactly 0, and the capped walk averages about 0.
feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Check the losing chance $(1 - p)^d$, and use one `rng.random()` per step.

byKey.error: Your code stopped with an error. Check that both `...` lines are replaced.

explain.text: The fair cycle is exactly 0 for any $d$; at the wheel it loses more as $d$ grows. The capped walk reaches $+1$ in about 92% of games and still averages near 0. The rare deep losses pay for the frequent small wins.

screens.title: Selling volatility
screens.prose: A book sells options far out of the money. Most days they expire worthless and it keeps a small premium. Rarely, a large market move makes one pay out a great deal. The chart is a sketch of such a P&L, not real data.
screens.question: Which statement about this book is right?

options.text: A hundred profitable days in a row prove the book has an edge
options.why: The doubling system also wins almost every cycle and has no edge. Long winning runs say nothing about the mean.

options.text: Its P&L has the doubling shape: many small gains, a rare large loss, and a mean that depends on both
It is safe, because the loss needs a rare event
options.why: Rare is not small. The loss is sized like doubling's £1,023.

options.text: A backtest over a calm year measures its mean well
options.why: A calm year may hold none of the rare losses, so it overstates the mean.

hints.text: Compare the chart with the doubling cycle.
Many small gains, then one large loss.
The mean must count the rare loss, which a short backtest may miss.

feedback.correct: Right: the same shape as doubling. Judge the mean with the rare loss in it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at what the small gains are paid for with.

byKey.edge: A winning streak is what this shape always shows before the loss.
byKey.rare: A rare loss can still cancel all the gains.
byKey.calm: The rare loss is the part a calm sample misses.

explain.text: Selling far out-of-the-money options earns a steady premium and carries a rare large loss, like doubling. Whether it has an edge depends on whether the premium covers the expected loss. A backtest without a bad day cannot answer that.

ideas: Stopping a fair walk at its first visit to $+1$ gives $E[S_T] = 1$. The cause: $E[T]$ is infinite and the losses on the way are unbounded.
Any floor or any cap on time restores $E[S_T] = 0$: the rare deep losses exactly pay for the frequent small gains.
Doubling with a finite bankroll is a bounded stop. Its mean is 0 at a fair coin and negative at a casino.

formula.note: Fair coin: 0. Red on a European wheel, $d = 10$: $-0.3056$.

summary.trap: A rare loss is not a small loss. Ten losses in a row are sized to cancel every win.

quiz.question: What is her expected P&L at the stop?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Is the stopping time bounded?

explain.text: $T \le 50$ is bounded, so optional stopping gives $E[S_T] = S_0 = 0$. However clever the rule, a bounded stop cannot beat a fair game.

quiz.prose: You double from £1 with a bankroll of £63 on a fair coin: at most six bets.
quiz.question: What is the chance that the cycle loses? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.correct: $(\tfrac12)^6 = \tfrac{1}{64}$, and the loss is £63, so the mean is 0.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. All six bets must lose.

byKey.ten: That is the ten-bet chance. Here you can afford only six bets.
byKey.six: $\tfrac16$ treats the six bets as one draw. Multiply six halves.

explain.text: Six losses in a row have chance $\tfrac{1}{64} \approx 0.0156$. The expected gain is $\tfrac{63}{64} \times 1 - \tfrac{1}{64} \times 63 = 0$.

quiz.prose: A fair walk from 0 stops at the first visit to $+1$, with no floor and no time cap.
quiz.question: Why does optional stopping not give $E[S_T] = 0$?

options.text: $T$ is unbounded, $E[T]$ is infinite, and the stopped walk is unbounded below
The walk is not a martingale
options.why: Each step is fair, so the walk is a martingale.

options.text: $T$ is not a stopping time
options.why: You know you have reached $+1$ the moment it happens, so $T$ is a stopping time.

options.text: The walk may never reach $+1$
options.why: The fair walk reaches $+1$ with chance 1.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check each condition of the theorem.

byKey.notstop: Reaching a level is decided by the past.

explain.text: With a floor at $-L$ the expected time is $L$, which grows without bound as the floor drops. So $E[T] = \infty$, $T$ is unbounded and so are the losses. With none of the conditions, $E[S_T] = 1$ is possible.
